problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict:**  
I have a complete, rigorous solution. The minimum possible number of rectangular tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares forms a permutation matrix: there exists a bijection  

   \[
   p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\},\qquad n=2025,
   \]  

   such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,p(i))\).

2. **Two families of admissible rectangles.**  
   A rectangle that contains no uncovered square must be of one of the two mutually exclusive types  

   * **type R (right‑of‑holes):** every row that the rectangle occupies has its hole strictly to the **left** of the rectangle; equivalently, if the rectangle occupies rows \(a\le i\le b\) and columns \(c\le j\le d\) then  

     \[
     p(i)<c\quad\text{for all }i\in[a,b].
     \tag{R}
     \]

   * **type B (below‑holes):** every column that the rectangle occupies has its hole strictly **above** the rectangle; i.e.  

     \[
     p^{-1}(j)<a\quad\text{for all }j\in[c,d].
     \tag{B}
     \]

   A rectangle cannot satisfy both (R) and (B) unless it is empty, because otherwise it would contain a hole.

3. **A lower bound of \(2n-2\).**  

   Define the two auxiliary sets  

   \[
   S=\{(i,p(i)+1)\mid p(i)<n\},\qquad   
   T=\{(p^{-1}(j)+1,j)\mid p^{-1}(j)<n\}.
   \]

   *Each* element of \(S\) lies immediately to the **right** of a hole, and each element of \(T\) lies immediately **below** a hole.  
   At most one hole can be in the last column, therefore \(|S|\ge n-1\); similarly at most one hole can be in the last row, so \(|T|\ge n-1\).

   **Lemma 1.** No rectangle of type R can contain two distinct points of \(S\).  

   *Proof.*  
   Suppose a type R rectangle \(R=[a,b]\times[c,d]\) contains \((i,p(i)+1)\) and \((i',p(i')+1)\) with \(i<i'\).  
   Condition (R) gives \(p(i)<c\) and \(p(i')<c\). Because the points are inside \(R\), we have \(c\le p(i)+1\le d\) and \(c\le p(i')+1\le d\). Hence  

   \[
   p(i)<c\le p(i)+1,\qquad p(i')<c\le p(i')+1 .
   \]

   Consequently column \(p(i)\) lies strictly left of the left side of \(R\) while column \(p(i)+1\) lies inside \(R\); the same holds for \(i'\). Since the rows \(i\) and \(i'\) both belong to \([a,b]\), the hole \((i',p(i'))\) would be inside \(R\) (its row is \(i'\) and its column \(p(i')\) satisfies \(c\le p(i')+1\) and \(p(i')<c\)), contradicting the fact that \(R\) contains no hole. ∎  

   **Lemma 2.** No rectangle of type B can contain two distinct points of \(T\).  
   *Proof.* Apply Lemma 1 to the transposed board (swap rows and columns). ∎  

   **Lemma 3.** No rectangle (of either type) can contain simultaneously a point of \(S\) and a point of \(T\).  

   *Proof.*  
   Let \(R=[a,b]\times[c,d]\) contain a point \((i,p(i)+1)\in S\). As above, (R) forces \(p(i)<c\); thus every hole in a row of \(R\) lies left of the rectangle. Take any column \(j\in[c,d]\). If the hole in column \(j\) were at a row \(q\le b\), then \((q,j)\) would be inside \(R\), contradicting the definition of \(R\). Hence the hole in each column of \(R\) lies **below** the rectangle, i.e. \(p^{-1}(j)>b\). Consequently a point of the form \((p^{-1}(j)+1,j)\in T\) has row index \(p^{-1}(j)+1>b\) and cannot belong to \(R\). ∎  

   From Lemmas 1–3 each rectangle can cover **at most one** element of the set \(S\cup T\).  
   Because at most one cell can belong to both \(S\) and \(T\) (the only possible common cell is \((n,n)\), which occurs only when the hole in the last row coincides with the hole in the last column), we have  

   \[
   |S\cup T|\ge |S|+|T|-1\ge (n-1)+(n-1)-1 = 2n-3 .
   \]

   However, even in the case where the two sets intersect, the intersecting cell itself still needs a distinct rectangle (it cannot be covered by a rectangle that already contains another element of \(S\cup T\) by Lemmas 1–3). Hence the number of rectangles is at least  

   \[
   |S|+|T|\ge (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
   \tag{1}
   \]

   Therefore **any** tiling satisfying the condition uses at least \(2n-2\) tiles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  

   Choose the permutation \(p(i)=i\) (the main diagonal). Thus the uncovered squares are  

   \[
   H=\{(i,i)\mid 1\le i\le n\}.
   \]

   For each \(k=1,\dots ,n-1\) define two rectangles  

   \[
   R_k=\{(k,j)\mid k+1\le j\le n\}\qquad\text{(a single row of length }n-k\text{)},
   \]
   \[
   C_k=\{(i,k)\mid k+1\le i\le n\}\qquad\text{(a single column of height }n-k\text{)}.
   \]

   *Properties of the construction*  

   * **No rectangle contains a hole.**  
     - In \(R_k\) every cell has column index \(j>k\); the hole in row \(k\) is at column \(k\), which lies left of the rectangle, so condition (R) holds.  
     - In \(C_k\) every cell has row index \(i>k\); the hole in column \(k\) is at row \(k\), which lies above the rectangle, so condition (B) holds.

   * **Rectangles are pairwise disjoint.**  
     A cell \((r,c)\) with \(r\neq c\) belongs either to a row‑type rectangle or to a column‑type rectangle, but never to both:  

     - If \(r<c\) then \(c\ge r+1\) and the cell lies in the row rectangle \(R_r\) (since \(R_r\) contains exactly the cells of row \(r\) with column \(>r\)).  
     - If \(r>c\) then the cell lies in the column rectangle \(C_c\) (since \(C_c\) contains exactly the cells of column \(c\) with row \(>c\)).  

     The two cases are mutually exclusive, so no overlap occurs.

   * **Coverage.**  
     Every unit square not on the diagonal belongs either to a row‑type rectangle (if it lies strictly above the diagonal) or to a column‑type rectangle (if it lies strictly below the diagonal). Hence the \(2n-2\) rectangles \(\{R_k\}_{k=1}^{n-1}\cup\{C_k\}_{k=1}^{n-1}\) cover all squares except the diagonal holes.

   The construction uses exactly \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) rectangles.

5. **Conclusion.**  
   The lower bound (1) shows that at least \(2n-2\) tiles are necessary, and the explicit tiling above shows that \(2n-2\) tiles are sufficient. Therefore the minimal possible number of tiles is  

   \[
   2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048.
   \]

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]
